What does Manton say about how a believer’s experience of God’s grace influences their desire for further communion with Him?

Manton teaches that tasting the Lord’s graciousness creates a yearning for more intimate fellowship. He explains that once a believer has "tasted that the Lord is gracious," this experience "kindles affection, and makes us long for more," leading to a renewed resolution to serve the Lord more faithfully and to walk in holiness. He further notes that "When you find benefit by one duty, it will be an encouragement to come again," indicating that each encounter with divine grace fuels a deeper desire for continued communion. [Manton — Works Vol14]

What does the sermon say about the responsibility of God's people in seeking the salvation of souls and the consequences of failing to do so?

Spurgeon teaches that believers are accountable for earnestly seeking the salvation of souls, warning that neglect brings severe accountability. He states, "if you who are His people are not earnest in seeking the salvation of souls, and they perish, their blood will be required at your hands!" The sermon underscores that while God’s sovereign will ultimately prevails, human earnestness in prayer and evangelism is essential; otherwise, the consequences fall upon the neglectful believers, as illustrated by the example of King Joash deciding whether the Syrians should be beaten three or six times. [Sermon 2303 — "Three Arrows--or Six?"]

What financial advantage does Cotton Mather claim the abolition of Popery would bring to England?

Mather argues that abolishing Popery would be a great economic benefit, noting that “the Abolifhing of Popery in England, is worth at Leaft Eight Millions of Pounds yearly to the Nation.” He presents this as a monetary incentive for embracing the Protestant religion. [Cotton Mather — Bonifacius Essays To Do Good]

According to Gill, how does God's providence relate to natural and necessary actions?

Gill teaches that the providence of God is concerned in all actions, "from the beginning to the end of it," and that He is a "God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1 Sam. 2:3). He explains that every muscular motion—such as birds flying, fish swimming, and humans walking—is continued by God's providence, because all motion ultimately comes from the first Mover, "in whom we live, and move, and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Gill further distinguishes that necessary actions either arise from the necessity of nature or are appointed by God's ordination. This shows that both natural activities and those required by nature are under divine governance. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

According to Ambrose in the passage titled “Looking Unto Jesus,” how does he contrast earthly pleasures with the believer’s true source of joy?

Ambrose teaches that the search for comfort and joy on earth is futile because the world is a place of suffering, not lasting happiness. He declares, "Earth is not the place for pleasure; earth is the place of sorrow, of trouble, of mourning, Jam. 5.5," and warns that the pleasures of the wicked are fleeting: "their Heaven is past; they spend their daies in wealth, or in mirth (saith Job ) of the wicked, and in a moment go down to the Grave." In contrast, the godly are called to look beyond the "vale of tears" to the eternal reward that awaits in heaven, as he exhorts, "Verily I say unto you, they have their reward; Mat. 6.2." Thus, Ambrose urges believers to abandon the pursuit of earthly comforts and fix their hope on the heavenly joy that surpasses all temporal afflictions. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

According to the passage, what is the wisest way for a believer to regard their own wisdom and strength?

Spurgeon teaches that the believer’s wisest approach is humility, urging them to "believe yourself neither to be wise nor strong" and to "lie humbly at His feet" so that God may make them both wise and strong. This posture guards against self‑conceit and the danger of being swept off one’s feet by temptation. [Sermon 2912 — "Comfort for Tried Believers"]

What examples does the passage give to show how people misunderstand the nature of sin?

Spurgeon illustrates the common misapprehension of sin by citing vivid, concrete examples. He recounts a Pharisee who defined sin as merely "it is eating without washing your hands. It is drinking wine without having first of all strained out the gnats," reducing moral failure to ritual impurity. He then contrasts this with a Spanish bandit who, after stabbing a man on a Friday, was more concerned that a few drops of blood had fallen on his lips and that he had "tasted animal food on a fast day," yet felt no remorse, noting that "the murder did not seem to arouse in his conscience any feeling of remorse at all--not one atom." These anecdotes demonstrate that many reduce sin to external actions while ignoring the deeper breach of conscience and divine law. [Sermon 812 — "The Deep-Seated Character of Sin"]

What reason does the passage give for a Christian to avoid consulting his enemy?

The passage teaches that a Christian must shun the counsel of his enemy because "It is God's enemy, and our enemy." Consulting an enemy is likened to taking a pirate to guide a ship, leading one away from good. Moreover, the apostle warns that living and deliberating according to the flesh results in death, as the text quotes: "If we live and deliberate ' according to the flesh, we shall die,' saith the apostle peremptorily." Hence, Christians are urged to renounce fleshly wisdom and avoid any imputation of carnal policy. [Sibbes — Works Vol03]

What mistake does the passage identify about people who think they should only pray?

The passage identifies a second mistake: it says that some people "think they are to doe nothing else but to pray, God hath commanded us to pray, and they thinke they are to doe nothing else," and consequently they "run to their knees, drop as it were a bead, say over a Pater Noster" at the expense of other duties. This error is portrayed as a neglect of the broader call to duty and the exercise of grace, reducing Christian life to prayer alone. [Bolton — True Bounds Of Christian Freedom]

What covenantal promise does Gill describe regarding believers being adopted as children of God?

Gill teaches that the covenant includes a promise that believers "should be openly adopted, and declared the children of God," meaning that God will treat them as His own offspring, granting them the status of His people, heirs, and portion. This adoption signifies a relational bond whereby God becomes their Father and they become His children, receiving both the discipline of the covenant rod and the inheritance promised to His people. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

How does Brooks describe the superiority of Christ’s riches compared to worldly wealth in this passage?

Brooks teaches that the riches of Christ are incomparable, stating that even a single "One grain of grace is far beyond all the gold of Ophir and all the silver of the Indies" and that worldly riches are merely "the guts and garbage of the earth." He further emphasizes the point by quoting Luther, who says, "The whole Turkish empire, is but a crust that Ged throws to a dog," illustrating that all earthly wealth is a mere burden when set against the priceless treasure of divine grace. [Brooks — Complete Works Vol3]

The sermon teaches that the 'sweet waters' of spiritual wisdom are accessible only to the refined and spiritual powers of the soul, and that the heart must be guided by divine direction. It states, "Those sweet waters could only be navigated by the heart and the heart itself would need Divine direction before it could find the entrance to them." Thus, true navigation depends on the indwelling of the heart and God's leading rather than mere intellectual belief. [Sermon 2028 — "The Love of God and the Patience of Christ"]

No physician, comforter, or even angels can succeed; when God speaks, the dying soul is revived and lifted from Hell to Heaven. [Swinnock — Incomparableness Of God]

What do the Canons of Dort say about the nature and scope of the decree of election?

The Canons of Dort teach that there is not a series of separate decrees of election but a single, unified decree that concerns all who will be saved under both the Old and New Testaments. They affirm that God, though the elect are "by nature neither better nor more deserving than others," has chosen them from eternity to receive grace, justification, sanctification, preservation, and ultimately glorification. This is expressed in the passage: "Whom he did predestinate, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified" (Rom. viii. 30). Thus, the decree of election is one consistent purpose of divine will that applies to the entire elect, leading them to holiness and glory for the praise of God's grace. [Reformed — Canons Of Dort]

What does the passage say about the nature of God's free grace?

The passage describes God's free grace as one that is given without merit, quoting the Scripture: "It is a free grace: Hosea xiv. 4, I will heal their backslidings, I will love them freely." It emphasizes that humanity was in a pitiful state by nature, yet God's grace is offered freely to heal and love, surpassing the law's condemnation. This free grace is presented as a foundational aspect of divine election and mercy. [Manton — Works Vol20]

What spiritual significance does the passage attribute to the refrain 'Sing unto the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously'?

Spurgeon teaches that the refrain is more than a historical hymn of Israel’s deliverance; it points to the ultimate overthrow of all evil powers and the final deliverance of the elect. He explains that the song will be sung by the redeemed "on the sea of glass, having the harps of God" at the close of the dispensation, celebrating both the literal overthrow of Egypt and the final triumph over the beast and his image. As he puts it, "It is obvious, then, from the plentiful allusions to this song in Holy Scripture, that it is full of deep spiritual significance." [Sermon 1867 — "Untitled Sermon"]

According to the passage, how does the timing of a believer's death relate to God's providence and the possibility of sudden death?

Spurgeon teaches that the Lord has fixed the hour of a believer’s entrance into rest, and that this timing cannot be altered by human skill or enemy malice. He affirms that “Plagues and death around us fly, Till He bids we cannot die,” indicating that no Satanic force can hurl the believer to the grave before the appointed time. Consequently, even if a believer were to die suddenly, it would merely be a transition from the lower room of the Father’s house to an upper, more glorious chamber, because those who walk in communion with God are always prepared for the moment of their passing. [Sermon 2039 — "Crossing the Jordan"]

How does the passage describe God's attitude toward the sacrifices and prayers of the wicked?

Spurgeon teaches that, according to the passage, God utterly detests the offerings of the ungodly, seeing them as a burden and an offense. He is described as having "I am perfectly sick of them, and weary of bearing them." The text explains that God does not merely reject these rites; He abhors them, considering their incense a hypocritical abomination and their assemblies a provocation. Thus, the divine response to wicked sacrifices is one of disgust and fatigue, not of gracious hearing. [Henry — Exposition Vol5]

According to the 1708 sermon, what are the three distinct ways the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers?

The sermon explains that the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers in a threefold manner. First, He is described as “the Holy Spirit was to be their Comforter, that they might not be afraid,” providing comfort and courage. Second, He serves as “their Advocate, that they might not be baffled,” defending and guiding them. Third, He operates as a divine power in communication: “When they spoke, there would be a power within them suggesting their words, a power with those words convincing their hearers, and a power in their hearers causing the word spoken to abide in their memories.” In this way the Spirit works within the speaker, persuades the listener, and secures the spoken word in memory. [Sermon 1708 — "The Holy Spirit's Threefold Conviction of Men"]

What characteristic does the passage say distinguishes the godly from the wicked?

The passage teaches that holiness is the mark that sets the godly apart from the wicked, stating that "As chastity distinguishes a virtuous woman from a harlot, so holiness distinguishes the godly from the wicked." It further describes holiness as "the badge and livery of God's people" and cites Scripture, "For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness" (1 Thess. iv. 7), emphasizing that true believers must reflect this divine calling. [Watson — All Things For Good]

According to the passage, how are believers instructed to show love to fellow godly persons?

The passage teaches that believers are to serve the godly "heartily, and with all faithfulnesse, as if it were for our selues" and to avoid slothfulness in service. It further advises that Christians should "care for their good and profit, as we would care for the good of the members of our owne body," recognizing the godly as members of the mystical body of Christ. By employing their spiritual gifts—knowledge, prayer, and other graces—for the benefit of others, and by sharing doctrine, psalms, and interpretations "for the profit of others," they fulfill their stewardship of God's manifold grace. Bayly teaches that when baptism is to be administered the observer should stay and behold it with reverent attention for six distinct purposes. First, the believer must “First, Shew thy reverence to God's ordinance;” thereby honoring the divine command. Second, one should consider “the better consider thine own ingrafting into the visible body of Christ's church,” reflecting on personal incorporation into the body of Christ. Third, the observer is to “repay thy debts, in praying for the infant which is to be baptized,” interceding that God grants the infant the inward effects of baptism. Fourth, the faithful should “assist the church in praising God for grafting another member into his mystical body,” joining the corporate worship. Fifth, the believer is to “prove whether the effects of Christ's death killeth sin in thee, and whether thou be raised to newness of life by the virtue of his resurrection,” examining the transformative power of the gospel. Sixth, one must “show thyself to be a freeman of Christ's corporation, having a voice or consent in the admission of others into that holy society,” affirming a participatory role in the church. These six purposes together shape a reverent and reflective posture toward baptism. [Bayly — Practice Of Piety]

The "wisdom of the world," in Paul's acceptation, refers to these gifts when they assume authority for themselves, refusing to be regulated by God's word or to yield in complete subjection to Him. If they set themselves in opposition to Christ, they are to be regarded as dangerous pests and hindrances. Therefore, an individual is considered wise in the world's account but foolish in God's estimation until they acknowledge that all true knowledge comes from God and resign themselves unreservedly to Christ's guidance. How does Howe illustrate the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs?

Howe illustrates the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs by explaining that the soul's very use of these organs implies an action antecedent to their assistance. He posits that the soul "supposes an operation upon them, antecedent to any operation by them." As an example, he notes that when one uses a pen, one first acts upon it to impress motion, an action that does not itself require another instrument. This suggests that the soul's action upon an organ must ultimately occur without the ministry of any organ, to avoid an infinite regress of bodies. Furthermore, Howe argues that even when separated from the body, the soul is not diminished but can still "perform those operations, which are proper to it self; that is, such as are more noble, and excellent, and immediately conducive to its own felicitie." He compares the soul's inability to perform "meaner, and grosser pieces of drudgerie" out of the body to a magistrate not personally executing a malefactor, emphasizing that this does not signify disparagement or diminution of its proper functions.
[Howe — Blessedness Of The Righteous]

Spurgeon highlights a stark contrast between the simple, truthful understanding of God's active involvement in creation, as taught in childhood, and the complex, God-excluding theories prevalent in a 'proudly enlightened age.' This truth, he argues, is being challenged by modern "schools of philosophy and science" that are "spinning all sorts of theories to get rid of God, to turn our Benefactor out of His own world and put man's best Friend as far away as possible." Spurgeon suggests that these skeptical teachers would benefit from returning to a simpler faith, recognizing that "our heavenly Father 'makes His sun to rise and He sends the rain,'" and that "Laws of Nature can do nothing without a power at the back of the laws."

What warning does William Gouge give about a husband who constantly commands his wife?

William Gouge warns that a husband who habitually commands his wife, without allowing persuasion or invitation, will eventually exhaust his own authority. He likens such over‑use of authority to “a swag gerers sword, which cannot long rest in the sheath, but vpon euery small occasion is drawne forth,” and observes that “Thus as by trying to bend steele how farre it will goe, it oft breaketh; so by putting their authoritie to the vttermost triall, they oft lose all their authoritie.” The remedy, he notes, lies in the husband’s own hands. [William Gouge — Of Domestical Duties]

What does Gill describe as the matter of satisfaction and how does Christ fulfill the law according to his doctrine?

Gill explains that the matter of satisfaction is ‘what that is which gives satisfaction to the justice of God; so that a sinner upon it, or in consideration of it, is acquitted and discharged.’ He argues that Christ accomplishes this by fulfilling the whole law in the place and stead of sinners. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

According to Morell, what are the two deductions that Priestley used to support his materialist view?

Morell reports that Priestley grounded his materialism on two logical deductions. The first deduction holds that thought and sensation are essentially identical, asserting that "the whole variety of our ideas, however abstract and refined they may become, are, nevertheless, but modifications of the sensational faculty." The second deduction claims that all sensation, and therefore all thought, originates from the affectations of our material organization, stating that it "consists entirely in the motion of the material particles of which the nerves and brain are composed." [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol1]

Dabney argues that the sin of the non‑elect cannot be the ground of their preterition because God’s foreknowledge of sin is a condition, not the cause, of divine decree. Calvin teaches that the term "mortal bodies" designates the portions of humanity that remain subject to death, which he describes as "the grosser part of us." He argues that this phrase does not refer to the final, instantaneous resurrection, but rather to the continual activity of the Holy Spirit that "gradually mortifies the relics of the flesh and renews in us a celestial life." What analogies does Spurgeon use in this sermon to illustrate how Christians can extract value from the words of a godless person?

Spurgeon teaches that even the utterances of a godless man can be valuable when they are "washed and carefully cleansed of the sand of sin--and what remains of golden grains may be turned to good account." These analogies show that believers should sift through sinful speech to retain the truth, just as one would keep a pearl or a diamond despite the filthy surroundings. [Sermon 1193 — "Girding on the Harness"]

What warning does Beveridge give about believers trying to determine their election by human reasoning?

Beveridge teaches that it is a grave error to make the certainty of election depend on human faith or on "posterior signs which are sure attestations to it." He warns that Satan tempts believers by sowing doubts about their election and by urging them to inquire "out of the proper way," meaning that they attempt to penetrate the hidden recesses of divine wisdom and understand the final determination God has made for them. In doing so, a person "plunges headlong into an immense abyss, involves himself in numberless inextricable snares, and buries himself in the thickest darkness," and the stupidity of the human mind is punished with fearful destruction. Thus, Beveridge cautions that seeking proof of one's election through speculative reasoning is the most perilous temptation for believers. [Institutes — Institutes Beveridge Vol2]

What does Gill say about the fate of the law in relation to the biblical statements that heaven and earth will pass away?

Gill teaches that the Scriptures affirm that the moral law will never be nullified, even though the created order is temporary. He notes that the first of those scriptures only says, "till heaven and earth pass", which will never be; and so not one jot or tittle of the law shall pass till all be fulfilled. Thus, while "heaven and earth shall pass away", the law endures until its ultimate fulfillment, and the passing of the world refers only to the temporary fashion and lusts of the age, not to the divine moral decree. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

Which early church fathers does Aa Hodge cite as supporting infant baptism as an apostolic tradition?

In Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology, Hodge records that several early Christian writers affirm infant baptism as an apostolic tradition. He notes that Justin Martyr (a.d. 138) says, "There were among Christians of his time, many persons of both sexes, some sixty and some seventy years old, who had been made disciples of Christ from their infancy." Irenaeus (born about a.d. 97) declares that "He came to save all by himself; all I say who by him are born again unto God, infants, and little children and youths." Origen (a.d. 185) observes that it was "the usage of the church to baptize infants," and adds that "the church had received the tradition from the apostles." Cyprian (bishop of Carthage, a.d. 248‑258) and his synod mandated infant baptism before the eighth day, and Augustine (a.d. 358) affirms that this "doctrine is held by the whole church, not instituted by councils, but always retained." Thus Hodge presents a continuous patristic witness to infant baptism as apostolic. [Systematic — Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology]

What two conditions does Hodge say Roman Catholic theology requires for a sacrament to be efficacious?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholic teaching holds the efficacy of a sacrament on the part of the administrator to two essential conditions. First, the minister must be "canonically authorized"—for the sacraments of orders and confirmation he must be a bishop in communion with the pope, and for the other sacraments he must be a regular popish priest; the personal character of the bishop or priest, even if he be in mortal sin, does not prevent the effect. Second, the minister must exercise the positive intention to do what the church intends, because "To the valid performance of the sacrament is required the intention upon the part of the officiating minister of doing that which the church does." [Systematic — Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology]

How does Spurgeon in Sermon 146 explain the proper way to assess a man's happiness?

Spurgeon teaches that true assessment of a man's happiness must include both his earthly life and his eternal destiny. According to Hodge, which sacraments do Roman Catholics regard as absolutely necessary for attaining salvation?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholics distinguish between absolute necessity and merely helpful means, and they hold that certain sacraments are absolutely necessary. He writes, "Baptism they hold to be absolutely necessary, either its actual reception, or the honest purpose to receive it, alike for infants and adults, as the sole means of attaining salvation." According to Gill, how is God's holiness compatible with the presence of sin in the world?

Gill teaches that God's holiness is displayed in his providential works, even when those works are dark and intricate, and that there is no criminal or sinful aspect in them. He emphasizes that the chief objection to God's holiness is the fact that sin exists, but asserts that God is "neither the author nor abettor of it; he neither commands it, nor approves of it, nor persuades to it, nor tempts nor forces to it." Rather, God forbids, disapproves, and chastises sin, yet overrules it for great good and His own glory, as seen in examples such as the fall of Adam and the crucifixion of Christ. Thus, the holiness of Jehovah the Father is observed in acts of grace, including the choosing of some in Christ to everlasting life before the world began. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

How does Spurgeon describe the willingness of modern churches to readmit a repentant brother compared to the early church at Corinth?

Spurgeon teaches that modern churches should be far more willing to restore a penitent member than the early church at Corinth, noting that "I scarcely know a Christian church that would refuse to receive into its membership again, a brother who had erred if he showed signs of true repentance." [Sermon 2918 — "Facing the Wind"]

What does the Greenham work say about the relationship between prayer, faith, and knowledge?

How does Sibbes explain the presence of lingering sin after a person has received pardon?

Sibbes teaches that even after pardon the root of sin may still linger like the dregs of a disease, because sanctification proceeds gradually and each prayer and renewal of repentance carries away some of the debt until the final physician—death—perfectly cures both soul and body. He affirms that this does not indicate weak grace, but divine wisdom, concluding that "God is wise. Let us not quarrel with our physician, for he is wiser than we ourselves." [Sibbes — Works Vol02]

What reason does Edwards give for why fore‑known events must actually exist, based on God's immutable knowledge?

Edwards argues that because God's knowledge is immutable, it cannot change or be succeeded by a new view; therefore any event that God foreknows cannot fail to exist. He explains that "the immutability of knowledge makes his knowledge to be without succession" and concludes that "it is utterly impossible the known events should fail of existence." Since a failure would require a change in God's knowledge, which is impossible, the existence of fore‑known events is guaranteed. [Edwards — Freedom Of The Will]

What twofold classification of keeping God's commandments does Manton give in Works Vol09, and how does he characterize the legal keeping?

Manton explains that there is "a twofold keeping or doing of the commandments — legal and evangelical." He describes the legal keeping as the exact obedience required by the rigor of the law, saying it is "when we do them so exactly as is answerable to the rigour of the law, and the rule of strict justice doth require, which exactness is when our obedience is universal in every point, when everything commanded by God is done by us without failing in one point." What does Calvin say is present in the Lord's Supper, and how does the Reformed view of the mode of reception differ from the Lutheran view?

Calvin teaches that the presence in the Lord's Supper is not the natural body and blood of Christ but "a supernatural, life-giving influence emanating from his glorified body in heaven, and conveyed to the believer by the power of the Holy Ghost." The Reformed position holds that the mode of reception is spiritual, with "the organ is not the mouth, but faith," and the condition of reception is the presence and exercise of faith, contrasting with the Lutheran view that the body and blood are received "corporaliter" through the mouth and actual consumption of the elements. [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol3]

What eight supports does Brooks provide for believers who have lost assurance?

Brooks outlines eight biblical supports for those who have lost assurance. The first is that “the great God might have burnt up all, he might not have left one house standing.” The second support is "That God has given them their lives for a prey." The third points to the common lot of sinners and saints. The fourth declares that even though believers have lost much as citizens, merchants, and tradesmen, they have lost nothing as “Cliristians, as they are saints, as they are the called of God.” The fifth assures that the Lord will certainly make up all their losses. The sixth promises that by fiery dispensations the Lord will make way for the new heavens and the new earth and the glorious deliverance of his people. The seventh foretells that God will bring about the ruin and destruction of his and his people's enemies. The eighth concludes that all shall end well and all shall work for good. [Brooks — Complete Works Vol6]

What does Ambrose say is the purpose of Christ’s ascension and sitting at the right hand of God?

Ambrose teaches that Christ’s ascent was not an end in itself but a preparation for the work of dispensing divine blessings to the saints. He explains that after rising, “Christ is gone up to heaven, Christ is set down at God's right hand,” where He is “invested with all the riches of Heaven” and holds “all the keyes of Heaven and Hell.” From that position He “gave gifts unto men, yea, he gave the gift of gifts, even the Holy Ghost himself,” so that believers may partake of that Spirit. Thus the purpose of the ascension is to enable Christ to bestow the Holy Spirit and all heavenly riches upon His people. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

What reason does Downame give for God requiring outward service in addition to inward piety?

Downame teaches that God does not rest solely on inward devotion, but "the Lord doth chiefly require and delight in the inward seruice of the soule, and the integrity and since rity of the heart; yet doth he not rest in it alone, but requi reth also the seruice of the body and outward man," so that the hidden righteousness of the heart may be manifested to others.
